body.heading: Same letters, different story
paragraphs: An anagram rearranges all the letters of a word or phrase to make a new one, using every letter exactly once. Some feel like fate: 'listen' becomes 'silent'. 'The eyes' becomes 'they see'. It is hard to believe those are accidents of spelling, which is exactly why anagrams delight us.
The rules matter. A true anagram adds nothing and drops nothing — if a letter is left over, it does not count. Spaces and punctuation are usually allowed to move or vanish; the letters are the law.

body.heading: Three to solve
paragraphs: Try these before reading the takeaway. First: 'triangle' — a shape hiding a word from maths class. Second: 'astronomer' — a person hiding what they watch, in two words. Third, an easy warm-up: 'night' hides a small object.

Work by fixing the vowels first, or by writing the letters in a circle and reading around it in different directions. Anagram solvers online exist, but the pleasure is in the moment the letters suddenly click into their second shape.

body.heading: Start your own anagram hunt
paragraphs: Names are the richest hunting ground — your own name may rearrange into something funny, grand or mysterious. Write the letters on separate slips of paper so you can slide them around; the hands often find what the eyes miss.
If you find a great one, you have a party trick for life. Just remember the golden rule when showing off: every letter, exactly once, or it is only a near-anagram wearing a costume.

takeaway: An anagram uses every letter exactly once — 'triangle' becomes 'integral', 'astronomer' becomes 'moon starer', and 'night' becomes 'thing'.
